A1: On July 1, according to the technology news outlet The Information, NVIDIA is providing financial guarantees to young cloud service providers that lease or rent its GPUs—if these companies fail to secure enough AI developers to rent their computing capacity, NVIDIA will repurchase their unsold GPU capacity at a pre-agreed price.

In return, NVIDIA will receive a percentage of these cloud providers’ revenue, with the revenue-sharing rate gradually declining over the term of the contract. GPU cloud providers Firmus and Sharon AI have already joined the program, and three executives with existing business ties to NVIDIA confirmed the arrangement.

On July 1, NVIDIA published a statement on its official website announcing a new business model that combines revenue sharing with credit support, enabling AI cloud providers to procure NVIDIA infrastructure without bearing the full upfront capital expenditure, and allowing them to offer computing services to downstream AI-native enterprises, model developers, and corporate clients.
A NVIDIA spokesperson also confirmed the existence of the program.

According to NVIDIA’s official press release, the company will earn not only standard product revenue but also an additional share of cloud service revenue, creating a usage-based, recurring revenue stream.

Sharon AI and Firmus are the first cloud providers participating in this model. Sharon AI plans to deploy up to 40,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GB300 GPUs, while Firmus is constructing a DSX AI Factory campus in Batam, Indonesia, expected to scale up to 360 megawatts and accommodate up to 170,000 NVIDIA GPUs.

The backstop sees Nvidia agreeing to rent back unused GPUs at a fixed rate.
Firmus and Sharon AI are among the first companies to have adopted the offer.
Firmus is deploying 170,000 GPUs in Batam, Indonesia, while Sharon AI is deploying 40,000 GB300 GPUs.

"Through the partnership, AI clouds will sell Nvidia-powered cloud services, with Nvidia earning both standard product revenue and a share of the cloud revenue on the supported capacity. This structure accelerates adoption of Nvidia platforms among the high-growth, high-conviction AI native sector, and provides Nvidia with a recurring, usage-linked earnings stream."
The agreement with CoreWeave was signed in September 2025 and had an initial value of $6.3bn , while the deal with Lambda was valued at $1.5bn .

article: Nvidia Vera Rubin rack costs $7.8M — memory is why

A1: Morgan Stanley Research estimates that Nvidia 's Vera Rubin VR200 NVL72 rack will cost hyperscale cloud providers around $7.8 million per unit, up from roughly $4 million for the current GB300 NVL72 generation.

Morgan Stanley puts memory content per rack at about $2 million, a 435% jump from the prior generation, driven by a threefold increase in LPDDR5X capacity to 54 terabytes per rack plus roughly $1 million or more in 3D NAND storage that was virtually absent from earlier systems.
As a share of the bill of materials, memory rose from 5 to 10 percent on the GB200 to 25 to 30 percent on the VR200, while the GPU's share fell from roughly 63 percent to 51 percent.
First shipments are scheduled for the third quarter of 2026, with volume ramping in the fourth.

gold_meaning.who: Bloomberg Intelligence survey (60 executives at Chinese software, finance, manufacturing and retail firms)
gold_meaning.what: share of AI accelerator budgets going to domestic (non-NVIDIA) products

A2:
Executives in the country say they will allocate 46 per cent of their budget for AI accelerators to domestic products over the next 12 months.
This is up from 30 per cent today, according to a Bloomberg Intelligence survey released on Tuesday (Jul 7).

While Nvidia’s products remain popular, the Santa Clara-based firm’s market share is expected to shrink as its H20 chips, which Beijing has urged its tech firms not to use , become harder to find and local firms take over, according to the survey.
At least 80 per cent of core technologies, such as chips, will be supplied by domestic companies, Bloomberg News reported.
